523f88cea1.q: What is the maximum total 401(k) contribution limit per year for any individual across all sources?
523f88cea1.a: The maximum you can put into your 401(k) per year is $61,000 for any individual. This comprises the employee contribution limit of $20,500, employer matching contributions, and after-tax contributions. If you contribute $61,000 annually earning 6% per year over 21 years, you accumulate approximately $2.4 million, or $3 million at 8% annual returns, making it a powerful tool for early retirement.

523f88cea1.rq: If you can do that every single year, you're going to have plenty of tax deferred money and plenty of Roth money and then when it comes to retirement you get to choose which bucket you take the money out of.

c6addd705c.q: How can you access 401(k) funds before age 59 and a half without penalty when retiring early?
c6addd705c.a: You can use 72(t) distributions, which require you to take substantially equal periodic payments from your 401(k) over the period between retirement and five years later, or until age 59 and a half, whichever is longer. Alternatively, if your plan allows and you retire from your current employer at age 55 or older, the Rule of 55 permits penalty-free withdrawals. Both strategies require specific calculations and cannot involve arbitrary withdrawal amounts.

4980086a61.q: What are the main one-time and ongoing expenses expecting parents should plan for before having a baby?
4980086a61.a: One-time expenses include medical and hospital bills from pregnancy and childbirth, a doula (optional), nursery items like a crib and bassinet, initial supplies like diapers, bottles, and formula. Ongoing expenses include childcare or nanny costs for dual-income families, potentially private school tuition from age six months through college, and increased emergency reserves because unexpected costs become more likely with a child. The key is stress-testing your budget by building a pretend monthly budget with these costs and living on it for a couple months before actually having the child.

35290fed64.q: How should couples evaluate whether their cash flow can support having a child?
35290fed64.a: Rather than asking how much you need to save before having a baby, the right question is what your cash flow can handle. A child is present from age zero through at least age 18, meaning you need 18 or more years of ongoing expenses, not just a one-time cost. You should look at your current cash flow and stress-test a pretend baby budget for a couple of months to see if you can stick to it. The strength of your ongoing cash flow may determine how financially ready you are to become a parent, and you must consider how childcare, schooling, and a potential mortgage or larger home fit together with all other expenses.
